facts.one_liner: Sandstone pillars and mesas above the Elbe, crossed by the famous Bastei Bridge.
facts.why_go: Saxon Switzerland, south-east of Dresden, is a landscape of sandstone towers, gorges and table mountains above the Elbe valley. The Bastei rock formation and its stone bridge, built in 1851, give classic views, while the Malerweg (Painters’ Way) trail follows the route that inspired Romantic artists. It is also a birthplace of free climbing, with more than a thousand climbing summits.
facts.best_time: May–October for hiking; autumn colours are spectacular.
facts.how_to_get_there: Trains from Dresden reach the area in about 30–40 minutes; Kurort Rathen is the closest station to the Bastei.
facts.good_to_know: The Bastei is busy at weekends—arrive early.

facts.one_liner: Five colourful villages clinging to terraced cliffs above the Ligurian Sea.
facts.why_go: Cinque Terre’s five villages—Monterosso, Vernazza, Corniglia, Manarola and Riomaggiore—sit on a rugged stretch of the Italian Riviera, linked by footpaths, trains and boats. Centuries of dry-stone terracing turned steep slopes into vineyards, and with Portovenere the area is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The Sentiero Azzurro coastal path gives famous views of pastel houses stacked above the sea.
facts.best_time: April–June and September–October for warm weather and fewer crowds.
facts.how_to_get_there: Trains on the La Spezia–Levanto line stop at all five villages; La Spezia is about 1.5 hours from Pisa airport.
facts.good_to_know: A Cinque Terre Card is needed for some trails—check which paths are open, as landslides can close sections.

facts.one_liner: Italy’s oldest national park, home to alpine ibex, glaciers and high meadows.
facts.why_go: Gran Paradiso became Italy’s first national park in 1922, growing out of a royal hunting reserve that saved the alpine ibex from extinction. Around the 4,061-metre Gran Paradiso massif, valleys such as Valnontey and Valsavarenche hold larch forests, waterfalls and old mule tracks built for King Victor Emmanuel II. Ibex and chamois are often seen close to the trails.
facts.best_time: June–September for hiking; winter for cross-country skiing in Cogne.
facts.how_to_get_there: Cogne is about 30 minutes’ drive from Aosta; Turin airport is about 2 hours away.
facts.good_to_know: Mountain huts book up in July and August—reserve ahead for overnight hikes.

facts.one_liner: White limestone cliffs and turquoise coves between Marseille and Cassis.
facts.why_go: Created in 2012, the Calanques National Park protects a stretch of Mediterranean coast where steep white limestone cliffs plunge into narrow, fjord-like inlets of turquoise water. Calanque d’En-Vau, Port-Pin and Sugiton are among the most beautiful, reached on foot via rocky trails or by boat from Marseille and Cassis. It is the only national park in Europe that is at once terrestrial, marine and on the edge of a major city.
facts.best_time: May–June and September–October; summer is hot and some areas close due to fire risk.
facts.how_to_get_there: Boat tours leave from Marseille’s Vieux-Port and from Cassis; trailheads are reached by bus or car from both.
facts.good_to_know: Access to massifs is restricted on high fire-risk days in summer, and reservations have been required for Sugiton in peak season—check the park website.

facts.one_liner: Wales’s highest mountains, glacial lakes and slate-grey valleys.
facts.why_go: Eryri, also known as Snowdonia, was designated in 1951 as Wales’s first national park. Its centrepiece is Yr Wyddfa (Snowdon), at 1,085 metres the highest mountain in Wales, with paths like the Pyg and Miners’ tracks passing glacial lakes such as Llyn Llydaw. The Snowdon Mountain Railway climbs to the summit in season, and the park also includes coastline, forests and villages like Betws-y-Coed and Beddgelert.
facts.best_time: May–September for the best hiking weather.
facts.how_to_get_there: Trains run to Bangor and Betws-y-Coed; the Snowdon Sherpa bus links trailheads around Yr Wyddfa.
facts.good_to_know: Weather on the summit can be severe even in summer. Car parks at Pen-y-Pass fill early—use the bus or book parking.

facts.one_liner: Lakes, oak woods and mountains on the Ring of Kerry.
facts.why_go: Killarney National Park was Ireland’s first national park and is a UNESCO Biosphere Reserve. Its three lakes are framed by Ireland’s highest mountains, the MacGillycuddy’s Reeks. Muckross House and gardens, Ross Castle, Torc Waterfall and the panorama from Ladies’ View are highlights, and the park is home to Ireland’s only native herd of red deer.
facts.best_time: May–September for long days; autumn brings colour to the woods.
facts.how_to_get_there: The park borders Killarney town, which has rail connections from Dublin and is about 20 minutes from Kerry Airport (KIR).
facts.good_to_know: Jaunting cars (horse-drawn carts) are a traditional way to tour—agree on the price before setting off.

facts.one_liner: Walk through the rift between the North American and Eurasian plates.
facts.why_go: Þingvellir is both a geological wonder and the birthplace of Iceland’s nation. The Althing, one of the world’s oldest parliaments, first met here in 930, and the site is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The park sits in a rift valley where the North American and Eurasian plates are pulling apart; the Almannagjá gorge and the Silfra fissure, where you can snorkel in clear glacial water, are highlights.
facts.best_time: June–August for long days; winter for snow and northern lights.
facts.how_to_get_there: About 45 minutes’ drive north-east of Reykjavík; it is the first stop on the Golden Circle route.
facts.good_to_know: Parking fees apply. Silfra snorkelling and diving require a licensed operator.

facts.one_liner: Limestone peaks, glacial lakes and Europe’s deepest canyon.
facts.why_go: Durmitor is a UNESCO World Heritage Site in northern Montenegro where 48 peaks rise over 2,000 metres. Glacial lakes like the Black Lake (Crno jezero) sit below the peaks, and the Tara River Canyon—about 1,300 metres deep—is Europe’s deepest. The Durmitor Ring road and the Sedlo Pass give stunning views, and rafting on the Tara is a classic adventure.
facts.best_time: June–September for hiking and rafting; winter for skiing in Žabljak.
facts.how_to_get_there: Žabljak is about 3 hours by road from Podgorica Airport (TGD).
facts.good_to_know: Mountain roads are narrow and winding. Rafting season peaks from May to September.

facts.one_liner: Travertine waterfalls cascading through a green river canyon.
facts.why_go: Krka National Park protects much of the Krka River in Dalmatia, where travertine barriers create a chain of waterfalls. Skradinski buk, the largest, is a series of 17 cascades surrounded by wooden walkways and old watermills. Further upstream, Roški slap and the island monastery of Visovac are reached by boat.
facts.best_time: May–June and September–October for fewer crowds; arrive early in summer.
facts.how_to_get_there: Skradin and Lozovac are the main entrances, about 20 minutes from Šibenik and about an hour from Split Airport (SPU).
facts.good_to_know: Swimming at Skradinski buk has been banned since 2021. Ticket prices are higher in peak season.

facts.one_liner: Sandstone gorges and Europe’s largest natural rock arch.
facts.why_go: Bohemian Switzerland borders Germany’s Saxon Switzerland and shares its dramatic sandstone landscape. Its icon is Pravčická brána, the largest natural sandstone arch in Europe, and boat rides through the narrow Kamenice gorges near Hřensko are a highlight.
facts.best_time: May–October for hiking and boat rides.
facts.how_to_get_there: Hřensko is about 2 hours by road from Prague or 45 minutes from Dresden; trains run to Děčín.
facts.good_to_know: Parts of the park were affected by a large wildfire in 2022—check which trails and boat rides are operating.

facts.one_liner: Austria’s highest peaks and the Pasterze, its longest glacier.
facts.why_go: Hohe Tauern is the largest national park in the Alps, spread across three Austrian states. It includes the Grossglockner, Austria’s highest mountain at 3,798 metres, and the Pasterze glacier at its foot. The Grossglockner High Alpine Road climbs to viewpoints like Kaiser-Franz-Josefs-Höhe, while the Krimml Waterfalls are among the highest in Europe.
facts.best_time: June–September; the Grossglockner High Alpine Road is usually open from May to early November.
facts.how_to_get_there: Heiligenblut and Fusch are the main gateways to the high alpine road; Salzburg is about 2 hours away.
facts.good_to_know: The high alpine road is a toll road. Weather above 2,000 metres changes quickly—bring warm layers.

facts.one_liner: One of the world’s best places to watch the northern lights, above the Arctic Circle.
facts.why_go: Abisko National Park lies about 200 km north of the Arctic Circle on the shores of Lake Torneträsk. Its ‘blue hole’—a patch of sky often clear when surrounding areas are cloudy—makes it a famous place for aurora watching. The park is also the start of the Kungsleden (King’s Trail), and in summer the midnight sun lights the mountains and canyons.
facts.best_time: September–March for northern lights; mid-June–mid-July for the midnight sun.
facts.how_to_get_there: Trains run from Kiruna (about 1.5 hours) and Narvik, Norway; the Kiruna Airport is about 1.5 hours by road.
facts.good_to_know: Winter temperatures can drop below −20°C. The Aurora Sky Station on Nuolja mountain is reached by chairlift.

facts.one_liner: Elephant herds beneath Mount Kilimanjaro’s snowy peak.
facts.why_go: Amboseli is known for its large elephant herds and its views of Mount Kilimanjaro across the border in Tanzania. Swamps fed by Kilimanjaro’s snowmelt attract elephants, buffalo, hippos and hundreds of bird species. Observation Hill gives a 360-degree view of the plains.
facts.best_time: June–October and January–February, the dry seasons, for the best wildlife viewing.
facts.how_to_get_there: About 4–5 hours by road from Nairobi, or a short flight from Wilson Airport.
facts.good_to_know: Kilimanjaro is often hidden by cloud—early mornings give the best views.

facts.one_liner: Cape Town’s flat-topped mountain, wrapped in clouds and fynbos.
facts.why_go: Table Mountain National Park stretches from Table Mountain itself to Cape Point. The mountain is famous for its ‘tablecloth’ of cloud. Its fynbos is part of the Cape Floral Region, a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Ride the cableway or hike Platteklip Gorge to the summit, visit the penguins at Boulders Beach, and stand at the Cape of Good Hope.
facts.best_time: October–April for summer weather; the cableway can close in high winds at any time of year.
facts.how_to_get_there: The lower cableway station is about 15 minutes from central Cape Town; Cape Town International Airport (CPT) is about 30 minutes away.
facts.good_to_know: Check cableway status before you go. Hike in groups and start early.

facts.one_liner: Jagged peaks and sheer escarpments home to gelada monkeys.
facts.why_go: The Simien Mountains are a UNESCO World Heritage Site with dramatic cliffs and peaks in the range that includes Ras Dashen, Ethiopia’s highest mountain. Gelada monkeys graze the high meadows, and rare Walia ibex and Ethiopian wolves live here too. Multi-day treks with scouts and mules pass viewpoints such as Imet Gogo and Chennek.
facts.best_time: October–March for clear skies; September for green landscapes after the rains.
facts.how_to_get_there: Debark is the gateway town, about 2–3 hours by road from Gondar.
facts.good_to_know: Treks require a park scout. Check the latest travel advisories before visiting.

facts.one_liner: A forest of razor-sharp limestone pinnacles crossed by rope bridges.
facts.why_go: Tsingy de Bemaraha is a UNESCO World Heritage Site in western Madagascar known for its ‘tsingy’—jagged limestone needles. Visitors use ladders, cables and suspension bridges to explore the Grand and Petit Tsingy, and lemurs live in the surrounding forest.
facts.best_time: May–November, the dry season; the park is often inaccessible in the rainy season.
facts.how_to_get_there: Bekopaka, the gateway village, is reached from Morondava by 4×4 (usually a full day’s drive).
facts.good_to_know: Guides are required. Wear gloves and sturdy shoes for the Grand Tsingy circuits.

facts.one_liner: Limestone karsts rising from emerald Cheow Lan Lake in ancient rainforest.
facts.why_go: Khao Sok protects one of Thailand’s oldest rainforests. At its heart, Cheow Lan Lake was created by the Ratchaprapha Dam, and its towering limestone karsts make it one of the country’s most spectacular sights. Stay in floating raft houses, kayak into caves, and look for gibbons and hornbills. The park is also home to Rafflesia flowers.
facts.best_time: December–April, the dry season.
facts.how_to_get_there: About 2 hours by road from Surat Thani or 3 hours from Phuket and Krabi.
facts.good_to_know: Lake trips are usually booked as tours with longtail boats.

facts.one_liner: Mount Fuji mirrored in lakes, hot springs and volcanic peninsulas.
facts.why_go: Fuji-Hakone-Izu National Park includes Mount Fuji, at 3,776 metres Japan’s highest peak, along with the Fuji Five Lakes, the hot-spring resort area of Hakone and the Izu Peninsula. Lake Kawaguchi gives classic views of Fuji, especially during the cherry blossom season.
facts.best_time: Late October–February for the clearest views; early April for cherry blossoms; July–early September for climbing Fuji.
